geometry.title: Reasoning with angles
lessons: Angle relationships

An angle measures the turn between two rays with a common endpoint. Adjacent angles share a vertex and side without overlapping interiors. A linear pair forms a straight angle, so its measures sum to 180°. Vertical angles are the opposite angles formed by intersecting lines; they have equal measures. Do not infer that two angles are equal merely because a drawing looks symmetric. Mark the relationship or justify it from a theorem.
Two adjacent angles form a line and measure 3x + 10 and 2x + 20 degrees. Their sum is 180: 5x + 30 = 180, so x = 30. The angles are 100° and 80°, which pass the sum check.
A linear pair measures 4x + 5 and 3x degrees. Find x and both angles. Explain why addition, rather than equality, is appropriate.
7x + 5 = 180 gives x = 25. The angles are 105° and 75°. They are supplementary, not necessarily congruent.
Parallel lines and transversals

A transversal crosses two lines at different points. When the lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, and same-side interior angles are supplementary. These conclusions require the parallel-line condition. Conversely, suitable equal corresponding or alternate interior angles can establish that two lines are parallel. Identify an angle's position before selecting a relationship.
If parallel lines create same-side interior angles of 110° and y°, then y = 70°. The alternate interior angle to the 110° angle instead measures 110°.
A transversal cuts parallel lines. One angle is 64°. Find its corresponding angle and its adjacent linear-pair angle. State each reason.
The corresponding angle is 64° by the parallel-lines theorem. The adjacent angle is 116° because a linear pair sums to 180°.
Proof and counterexamples

A proof connects accepted definitions, postulates, and established theorems to a claim through justified steps. A diagram suggests relationships but does not prove them. To disprove a universal claim, one valid counterexample is sufficient. To prove it, checking a few examples is not sufficient. The converse of a true conditional need not be true; distinguish 'if P then Q' from 'if Q then P.'
Every square is a rectangle because a square has four right angles. The converse fails: a rectangle with side lengths 2 and 5 has four right angles but is not a square.
Evaluate: 'If two angles are congruent, they are vertical angles.' Give a counterexample and identify the true related theorem.
Two separate right angles are congruent but need not be opposite angles at an intersection. Vertical angles are congruent; the converse is false.

geometry.title: Triangles and congruence
lessons: Triangle angle sums

In Euclidean geometry, the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two nonadjacent interior angles. The exterior angle forms a linear pair with the adjacent interior angle. When solving, distinguish an exterior measure from an interior measure instead of placing every number directly into a 180° equation.
A triangle has interior angles 48° and 67°. Its third angle is 180 − 48 − 67 = 65°. The exterior angle at that third vertex is 115°, also equal to 48 + 67.
A triangle has angles x, 2x, and 3x degrees. Find the angles and the exterior angle at the largest angle.
6x = 180, so x = 30. The angles are 30°, 60°, 90°. The exterior angle adjacent to 90° is 90°.
Congruence criteria

Congruent triangles have matching corresponding sides and angles. SSS, SAS, and ASA are sufficient criteria; AAS follows using the angle sum. In SAS, the specified angle must be between the two specified sides. Three equal angle pairs establish similarity, not necessarily congruence. SSA does not generally determine a unique triangle. Match vertices in a consistent order before writing a congruence statement.
If AB = DE, AC = DF, and angle BAC = angle EDF, the included angles match and the triangles ABC and DEF are congruent by SAS. The vertex correspondence is A↔D, B↔E, C↔F.
Two triangles have angle measures 40°, 60°, and 80°. Must they be congruent? Describe a construction that tests your claim.
No. Enlarge one triangle by scale factor 2. Its angles stay equal while its side lengths double. AAA establishes similarity, not congruence.
Isosceles triangles and midsegments

An isosceles triangle has at least two congruent sides, and the angles opposite those sides are congruent. A triangle midsegment joins the midpoints of two sides. It is parallel to the third side and half its length. These statements refer to corresponding sides and angles; label the diagram so the equal sides are not confused with the base.
An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 44°. Each base angle measures (180 − 44)/2 = 68°. A midsegment parallel to a 14 cm base measures 7 cm.
An isosceles triangle has base angles of 72°. Find its vertex angle. A midsegment parallel to its base is 9 cm; find the base.
The vertex angle is 180 − 144 = 36°. The base is twice the midsegment, so it measures 18 cm.

geometry.title: Similarity and right triangles
lessons: Scale factors and similarity

Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding lengths. A dilation multiplies lengths by a positive scale factor k. Perimeters scale by k, areas by k², and volumes of similar solids by k³. Ratios must compare corresponding measurements in a consistent direction. Similar triangles can be established by AA; matching angles does not establish equal size.
A map triangle has sides 3, 4, and 5 cm. A similar triangle with shortest side 9 cm has scale factor 3, so its other sides are 12 and 15 cm. Its area is nine times the original area.
Two similar rectangles have corresponding widths 4 and 10. If the smaller area is 24 square units, find the larger area and explain the exponent.
The length factor is 10/4 = 2.5. Area uses two dimensions, so its factor is 2.5² = 6.25. The larger area is 150 square units.
The Pythagorean theorem

For a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c². The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side. The converse can test whether a triangle is right. The theorem does not apply to arbitrary triangles. Keep exact radicals when possible and check that a computed hypotenuse exceeds either leg.
A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. Then c² = 36 + 64 = 100, so c = 10. If a triangle instead has sides 6, 8, and 11, it is not right because 6² + 8² ≠ 11².
A ladder 13 ft long reaches a wall while its base is 5 ft from the wall. Assuming a right angle at the ground, how high does it reach?
The ladder is the hypotenuse. Height² = 13² − 5² = 144, so height = 12 ft. Adding the squares would incorrectly treat a leg as the hypotenuse.
Right-triangle trigonometry

For an acute angle θ in a right triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Opposite and adjacent depend on which acute angle is selected. The hypotenuse does not change. Ratios are determined by the angle because right triangles with the same acute angle are similar. Use degree mode for degree measures.
In a 3–4–5 triangle, choose the angle opposite the side of length 3. Its sine is 3/5, cosine is 4/5, and tangent is 3/4.
For the other acute angle of the same 3–4–5 triangle, give sine, cosine, and tangent. Explain what swaps.
Sine = 4/5, cosine = 3/5, tangent = 4/3. Opposite and adjacent swap when the reference angle changes; the hypotenuse remains 5.

geometry.title: Circles and coordinates
lessons: Arcs and circle angles

A central angle has its vertex at a circle's center; its degree measure equals that of its intercepted minor arc. An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle and measures half its intercepted arc. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency. Specify the intercepted arc: an angle can intercept a major arc even when the picture emphasizes a minor one.
An inscribed angle intercepting an 80° arc measures 40°. A central angle intercepting the same arc measures 80°. An angle inscribed in a semicircle measures 90° because its intercepted arc is 180°.
An inscribed angle measures 57°. Find its intercepted arc and a central angle intercepting that same arc.
The intercepted arc is 114°. The central angle is also 114°. Doubling applies to the inscribed angle, not to an already-central angle.
Circle length and area

A circle with radius r has circumference 2πr and area πr². A sector occupying angle θ degrees is θ/360 of the full circle, so its arc length and area use that fraction. Radius and diameter are different: d = 2r. Length uses linear units and area uses square units. Leave π exact until the final approximation. A complete circle is 360° or 2π radians; identify the angle unit before choosing a formula.
For radius 6 and central angle 60°, arc length = (60/360)(12π) = 2π. Sector area = (60/360)(36π) = 6π square units.
A circle has diameter 10 cm. Find the circumference and the area of a 90° sector.
The radius is 5 cm. Circumference = 10π cm. The sector area is (1/4)(25π) = 25π/4 cm².
Distance, midpoint, and circles

The distance formula comes from the Pythagorean theorem: distance² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)². The midpoint averages each coordinate. A circle centered at (h,k) with radius r has equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². The signs inside the parentheses are opposite the center's coordinates.
The midpoint of (−2,1) and (4,9) is (1,5), and their distance is √(6² + 8²) = 10. A circle centered at (1,5) with radius 5 has equation (x − 1)² + (y − 5)² = 25.
Find the center and radius of (x + 3)² + (y − 2)² = 49. Test whether (4,2) lies on it.
The center is (−3,2), the radius is 7. Substitution gives 7² + 0² = 49, so (4,2) lies on the circle.

geometry.title: Measurement and transformations
lessons: Area by decomposition

A composite region can be partitioned into familiar nonoverlapping shapes or found by subtracting a missing region. A triangle's area is one half base times perpendicular height; a parallelogram's area is base times perpendicular height. The slanted side is not necessarily the height. State units, and check that the result is smaller than an enclosing rectangle when appropriate.
A 10 by 8 rectangle has a right-triangle corner removed with perpendicular legs 4 and 3. The remaining area is 80 − (1/2)(4)(3) = 74 square units.
A parallelogram has base 12, perpendicular height 5, and slanted side 7. Find its area and perimeter, explaining why different measurements are used.
Area = 12×5 = 60 square units. Perimeter = 2(12 + 7) = 38 units. Height measures separation between parallel bases, not boundary length.
Volumes and surface areas

Volume measures three-dimensional space in cubic units. A prism has volume Bh, where B is base area and h is perpendicular height. A cylinder follows the same rule with circular base area πr². A pyramid or cone with the same base area and height has one third the corresponding prism or cylinder volume. Surface area instead measures the exposed two-dimensional boundary.
A cylinder of radius 3 and height 10 has volume 90π cubic units. Its total surface area is 2πr² + 2πrh = 18π + 60π = 78π square units.
Compare a cone and cylinder with radius 4 and height 9. Find each volume, with units.
Cylinder volume = π(4²)(9) = 144π cubic units. Cone volume = (1/3)(144π) = 48π cubic units. The one-third relation assumes equal base areas and heights.
Rigid motions and symmetry

Translations, rotations, and reflections preserve lengths and angle measures, so they preserve congruence. A translation adds the same coordinate displacement to every point. Reflection across the x-axis maps (x,y) to (x,−y); reflection across the y-axis maps it to (−x,y). A 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin maps (x,y) to (−y,x). A dilation generally preserves shape but not size.
Point (2,−3) reflected across the x-axis becomes (2,3). Rotating that image 90° counterclockwise about the origin gives (−3,2). Reversing these operations can give a different result.
Translate (−1,4) by (3,−2), then reflect across the y-axis. Give both intermediate and final points and identify what remains invariant.
Translation gives (2,2); reflection gives (−2,2). Distances and angles are preserved by both transformations, although orientation reverses under reflection.

prep-computer-science-a.title: Values and expressions
lessons: Java types and assignment

Java variables have declared types. An int stores an integer in a finite range; a double represents floating-point values approximately; a boolean stores true or false. Assignment evaluates the right-hand expression and stores the result in the variable on the left. Assignment is not an algebraic equality that remains true after another variable changes. Local variables must be initialized before use. These examples use long-established Java language features, not preview features.
int a = 4; int b = a; a = 9; leaves b equal to 4. The earlier assignment copied the value; it did not permanently connect the variables.
Trace int x = 6; int y = x + 2; x = y - 1;. Give the final values and explain evaluation order.
y is assigned 8. Then x is assigned 7. Each statement uses the values available when that statement executes.
Arithmetic and integer division

Java evaluates multiplication, division, and remainder before addition and subtraction, unless parentheses change the grouping. Division of two int values produces an integer quotient truncated toward zero. A double operand makes the numeric division floating point. Casting after an integer division does not restore its discarded fractional part. The remainder operator gives the remainder for integer arithmetic.
7 / 2 is 3, while 7 / 2.0 is 3.5. (double)(7 / 2) is 3.0 because integer division happened first. (double)7 / 2 is 3.5.
Evaluate 17 / 5, 17 % 5, and (double)17 / 5. Explain why the three results differ.
The values are 3, 2, and 3.4. Integer quotient and remainder satisfy 17 = 5×3 + 2. The cast changes the division's operand type.
Strings and concatenation

String is a reference type representing an immutable sequence of characters. Concatenation with + joins text, including the text representation of numeric operands. Addition and concatenation group left to right, so parentheses can change a result. Use .equals to compare String contents; == compares reference identity for objects. Do not rely on string interning to make == appear reliable.
"Score: " + 2 + 3 yields "Score: 23". "Score: " + (2 + 3) yields "Score: 5" because the numeric addition occurs first.
Predict the text of 2 + 3 + " points" and "points " + 2 + 3. How should two independently created Strings be compared for equal text?
The texts are "5 points" and "points 23". Use first.equals(second) when first is non-null, or a null-safe equality helper.

prep-computer-science-a.title: Decisions and logic
lessons: Boolean expressions

Relational operators compare values and produce booleans. && requires both operands to be true; || requires at least one; ! negates a boolean. Java short-circuits && and ||: it may skip the right operand when the left already determines the result. Parentheses make intended grouping clear. Avoid confusing =, assignment, with ==, an equality comparison.
If x = 0, x != 0 && 10 / x > 2 is false without dividing by zero. The left operand is false, so Java does not evaluate the right operand.
For a = true and b = false, evaluate !(a && b) and !a && !b. Are they equivalent for all inputs?
The first is true; the second is false. They are not equivalent. De Morgan's law gives !(a && b) equivalent to !a || !b.
Selection and boundary cases

An if statement chooses an action based on a boolean condition. An if/else chain executes the first matching branch and skips later branches. Separate if statements are tested independently. Test boundary values exactly at thresholds and just to either side. Braces make branch ownership explicit and prevent mistakes when statements are added.
For if (score >= 90) grade = "A"; else if (score >= 80) grade = "B"; else grade = "C";, a score of 90 follows the first branch.
Design a mutually exclusive condition chain for negative, zero, and positive integers. Show which branch handles −1, 0, and 1.
Use if (n < 0), else if (n == 0), else. The three cases are disjoint and cover every int. Values −1, 0, and 1 exercise all branches.
Tracing nested conditions

Nested conditionals require tracking both the outer and inner decisions. Indentation helps readers but braces determine structure. A useful trace table records variable values, each evaluated condition, and any output. Do not execute branches that were skipped. Reasoning with a table is more reliable than guessing from the last line of code.
If x = 5 and y = 2, then if (x > 0) { if (y > x) x = y; else y = x; } sets y to 5 and leaves x at 5. The else belongs to the inner if.
Trace the same code when x = −1 and y = 8. Which comparisons execute, and which variables change?
Only x > 0 executes, and it is false. The entire inner block is skipped. x stays −1 and y stays 8.

prep-computer-science-a.title: Iteration and algorithms
lessons: Count-controlled loops

A for loop evaluates its initializer once, then checks the condition before each iteration, executes the body, and performs the update. The condition determines whether an endpoint is included. Loops with index < length visit indices 0 through length−1. Track how many times the body executes rather than counting punctuation or condition checks.
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) executes with i equal to 0, 1, 2, and 3. The body runs four times; the condition is checked a fifth time and fails.
How many times does for (int i = 2; i <= 10; i += 2) execute? List every value of i used in its body.
It executes five times, using 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10. The next update gives 12, which fails the condition.
Accumulators and invariants

An accumulator combines values across iterations. Initialize it to an identity appropriate to the operation: zero for a sum, one for a product. A loop invariant describes a fact maintained through iterations and can justify the final answer. Be careful not to reset an accumulator inside the loop unless that reset is intentional.
int sum = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) sum += i; produces partial sums 1, 3, 6, 10. After processing i, sum equals 1 + 2 + ... + i.
Trace int product = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) product *= i;. Explain what would happen if product began at zero.
The partial products are 1, 2, 6, 24. Starting at zero keeps every product zero, so the multiplicative identity must be 1.
While loops and termination

A while loop checks its condition before each body execution and can execute zero times. A correct loop needs progress toward a condition that eventually becomes false, unless indefinite operation is intentional. For a search, check bounds before using an index. Short-circuit evaluation helps guard array access. A termination argument should specify what changes and why it cannot continue forever.
int n = 20; while (n > 1) n /= 2; visits body-start values 20, 10, 5, and 2, ending at 1. Positive integer division makes n smaller each time.
Trace int n = 3; int count = 0; while (n < 20) { n *= 2; count++; }. Give final values and a termination argument.
n takes 6, 12, and 24; count ends at 3. Doubling a positive integer eventually crosses this finite threshold, with these small values avoiding overflow.

prep-computer-science-a.title: Objects and methods
lessons: Methods and parameters

A method defines a named computation. Parameters receive copies of argument values when the method is called. A non-void method returns a value compatible with its return type. Local variables belong to their method invocation. Changing a primitive parameter does not change the caller's primitive variable. Separate a method's returned value from any output it prints.
static int twice(int n) { n = n * 2; return n; } returns 8 for argument 4. If int x = 4; int y = twice(x);, x remains 4 and y becomes 8.
For static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }, trace int x = 3; int z = add(x, x + 1);. What are x and z?
Arguments evaluate to 3 and 4; the method returns 7. x remains 3 because the method receives values, not a writable alias to the caller's local variable.
Classes and encapsulation

A class defines a type with fields and behavior. Each ordinary object has its own instance-field values. Constructors initialize new instances. Private fields and public methods can protect valid state, but a class is not automatically correct just because fields are private. Describe an invariant, such as a balance never being negative, and make each modifying method preserve it.

Two Counter objects can each hold a private int value. Incrementing one object's field does not change the other's field. A static field, in contrast, belongs to the class rather than to each individual object.
A BankAccount stores a nonnegative balance. What must a withdrawal method check before subtracting an amount? Include a negative-amount case.

It must reject negative withdrawals and withdrawals exceeding the balance. Otherwise subtracting a negative amount could improperly increase the balance, or excessive withdrawal could break the invariant.
References and aliases

A variable of a reference type holds a reference to an object, or null. Assigning one reference variable to another does not copy the object. Both variables can refer to the same mutable object, so a mutation through one is visible through the other. Reassigning one variable to a different object changes only that variable's reference. Drawing arrows from variables to objects clarifies this distinction.
If Counter b = a; and both refer to one Counter, b.increment() changes that object's value, observable through a. But b = new Counter(); makes b refer to a new object without moving a.
Create a reference diagram for Counter a = new Counter(); Counter b = a; b = new Counter();. How many objects exist, and are a and b aliases at the end?
Two Counter objects were created. Initially a and b were aliases; after b's reassignment they refer to different objects.

prep-computer-science-a.title: Arrays and analysis
lessons: Array indices and traversal

A Java array has a fixed length and zero-based indices. For an array of length n, valid indices are 0 through n−1. Accessing an invalid index throws an exception. A standard indexed traversal uses i < values.length. An enhanced for loop is convenient for reading elements, but assigning a new value to its primitive loop variable does not replace the corresponding array element.
For int[] values = {2, 4, 6};, values.length is 3 and values[2] is 6. values[3] is outside the bounds. To double the elements, an indexed assignment values[i] *= 2 changes the array.
Trace int[] a = {1, 3, 5}; for (int v : a) { v *= 2; }. What does a contain afterward, and how would you actually double its elements?
a still contains 1, 3, 5. Use for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] *= 2; to replace each element.
Searching and edge cases

Linear search checks elements one by one and can stop when a match is found. If no match appears, it reports absence explicitly, often using −1 for an index. Test an empty array, a match at either end, duplicates, and no match. Binary search requires sorted data and a consistently shrinking search interval; applying it to an unsorted array is not reliable.
Searching {8, 3, 8, 1} from left to right for 8 returns index 0 if the algorithm stops on its first match. A different specification might request every match, so define the desired result first.
Write pseudocode to return the first index of target in an array, or −1. Explain its worst-case number of element comparisons for length n.
Visit indices 0 through n−1; return i when values[i] equals target; return −1 after the loop. The worst case uses n comparisons when the match is last or absent.
Nested loops and complexity

Nested loops combine repetitions. If an outer loop executes n times and each iteration runs an inner loop m times, the inner body executes n×m times. If the inner bound depends on the outer index, sum the varying counts rather than multiplying by a fixed bound. Big-O describes asymptotic growth, not an exact measured runtime on a phone or laptop.
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) visits n² pairs. If instead j starts at i + 1, it visits n(n−1)/2 distinct unordered index pairs, still O(n²).
For n = 4, count executions when i ranges 0..<n and j ranges 0..<i. List the count contributed by each outer iteration.
The contributions are 0, 1, 2, and 3, totaling 6 = n(n−1)/2. The bound grows quadratically even though fewer than n² bodies execute.
